content.thinking:
I need to write this postmortem without typing any raw figures myself, substituting placeholder names in braces wherever a number or digit would appear, while keeping labels and text otherwise natural.

Tracing the causal chain: account pages failed because calls to the payment provider returned 503s, the provider itself began erroring out with no corresponding production changes on our side, pointing to a third-party outage compounded by io-shop's synchronous dependency with no fallback. I should note contributing factors like the lack of mitigation options and a proposed fix PR whose contents I can't verify, so I won't claim what it does.

I'm drafting concrete action items: making the card section degrade gracefully on provider failure, adding a runbook for disabling card lookups during upstream outages, and alerting specifically on payment provider 503 rates to close the detection gap I calculated earlier. For lessons learned, I want to credit quick identification of the upstream cause while flagging what's unverified — the PR contents, the duration's lower bound, and whether the disconnect errors are truly unrelated noise.

I'm tracing the five-whys down to root cause: io-pay returned the Gbf7d.1 error during card lookup, and the account page renders this synchronously with no fallback path — treating this as a hypothesis sourced from the service register rather than confirmed fact, since the provider's own status isn't verified. I'm keeping the executive summary free of specific component names.

action_items.item: Make the account page degrade gracefully when the payment provider fails. Put a timeout and circuit breaker on the card lookup and render the page without card details instead of failing the request.
Give Argus a mitigation for upstream-dependency failures, for example a flag that switches off the card lookup on the account page, plus a runbook entry saying when to use it.
Add an alert on the rate of error responses from the payment provider, so a provider outage is flagged before or alongside the user-facing error-rate page.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers opening the account page got errors. The error rate rose from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken} on average and peaked at {errors_at_worst}, starting at {began}, and it had not recovered by the last minute read.

Account page requests failed because io-shop's call to the payment provider's card endpoint came back with {Gbf7d.1} errors. The log lines show this from the onset onward. The few client-disconnect errors are a separate, small background noise.
The payment provider began returning {Gbf7d.1} errors from {C1.2}. No production change and no flag change preceded the onset, so the fault is not an internal deploy or configuration change.

The provider's failure turned into a page failure because the account page fetches card data from it synchronously while rendering, and a failed lookup fails the whole request. There is no timeout, fallback or degraded page. The service register lists the provider as an external dependency, and the failing call is in the payment provider client code.
Why the provider itself began failing is not answered by the record. The candidate was never tested and the provider's own status was not read.

contributing_factors.factor: The account page has a hard synchronous dependency on the payment provider with no graceful degradation, so a provider outage takes down the whole page.
Argus has no mitigation for an upstream-dependency failure and refused to act. Recovery depended on the provider or on a human acting on the code fix.
Detection was slow and indirect. The alert fired {alert_raised - began} after the onset, and only on io-shop's own error rate, with nothing watching the provider's error responses.

input.executive_summary: From {began}, shoppers who opened their account page mostly got errors. About {errors_while_broken} of requests failed on average, against {errors_before} beforehand, and at the worst point every request failed. The service had not recovered when the last metrics were read, so the outage lasted at least {duration}. The cause appears to be an outage at the external payment provider the account page depends on. Nothing changed on our side. Argus found no safe automatic mitigation, so it handed the incident to the code-fix step, which opened a draft pull request. A human then took over, and Argus held the incident for {held}. The draft fix still has to be reviewed, and the provider may still be failing.

went_well: The Investigator placed the onset from the metrics and quickly tied the failures to the provider's error responses in the logs, and it ruled out recent deploys and flag changes.
Argus did not take a mitigation that would not have helped. It refused to act and moved on to the code-fix step, which opened a draft pull request for a human.
went_wrong: Nothing Argus could do addressed the failure, so users stayed affected through the whole response and the outage had not ended when the incident closed.
The page failing completely when only the card lookup fails was a design weakness that turned a partial third-party outage into a broad one.
The only candidate was never tried, and the provider's status was never checked, so the root cause remains unconfirmed.

input.root_cause: The third-party payment provider (io-pay) began answering the card lookup with {Gbf7d.1} errors from about {began}. The io-shop account page calls that lookup synchronously while rendering and has no fallback, so every provider failure became a failed page. The reason the provider failed is outside our evidence.
input.symptom: Account pages mostly failed to load
